vignette:
At 21, she works long days in the forest, moving through marked trails with a radio clipped to her vest, checking for disease in young trees and watching for signs of fire risk. She says she used to love how quiet the woods could be, the kind of quiet that made her feel steadier inside. Now she notices every snapped branch, every distant shout, every engine in the distance. Even in a place other people find peaceful, her body rarely settles.

The change begins the summer before, on a dry afternoon at a public campground near the edge of the forest district where she is training. She is there with two other workers, helping redirect visitors away from a closed trail after a storm. Families are packing up late lunches, children are running between picnic tables, and she remembers feeling bored and sunburned and eager for the shift to end. Then she hears screaming from across the lot. At first she thinks it is children playing, but the sound sharpens quickly into panic. She turns and sees a man striking a woman beside an SUV while a small child stands nearby crying. The image fixes in her mind with unnatural clarity: the woman's head hitting the side of the car, the child's open mouth, the man's face seeming both ordinary and terrifying.

She freezes for a moment that still shames her. One of her coworkers yells and starts running forward. She fumbles for her radio, her hands suddenly numb and clumsy, and by the time she speaks her voice sounds strange to her, thin and far away. Other campers begin shouting. The man gets into the vehicle and drives off before police arrive. She stays with the woman until paramedics come, kneeling in gravel beside her, answering questions she can barely process. The child's crying does not stop. That sound follows her home more than anything else.

For the first few days she tells herself she is just rattled. Her family, who immigrated when she was young, urge her to rest and pray and be grateful she was not physically harmed. She agrees, because on paper that seems true. But sleep changes almost immediately. When she closes her eyes, the scene starts again before she can stop it. Sometimes in the dream she is the one being struck; sometimes she is still standing frozen, unable to move while the child looks at her. She wakes with her heart racing, already alert, as if she has overslept for danger.

At work, she starts avoiding campgrounds and visitor contact when she can. She tells her supervisor she prefers remote survey assignments, framing it as independence and efficiency. Out in the forest she functions well enough if she is alone and moving. She can measure saplings, log pest damage, mark coordinates. But if she hears raised voices from hikers on a nearby trail, her stomach drops and her attention disappears. Once, when a couple argues near a trailhead, she leaves her equipment where it is and circles back through brush to avoid passing them. She feels embarrassed afterward, angry at herself for acting "ridiculous," yet unable to do differently in the moment.

Her mind keeps returning to the child. She scans parking areas automatically now, noticing where families stand, whether anyone seems tense, whether a car door is open too hard. She watches men's hands without meaning to. If someone steps quickly out from behind a vehicle, her body reacts before her thoughts catch up. On two occasions she has dropped to the ground at sudden noise, then stood up pretending she was tying her boot. She laughs when coworkers joke about her being "jumpy," but the laughter costs effort.

She has become more withdrawn with friends, especially when they want to go to busy outdoor recreation areas after work. She makes excuses, saying she is tired or has an early start. In truth, crowded parking lots and family noise make her chest tighten. Her younger brother recently asked why she no longer comes to his soccer games, and she cannot explain that the shouting from sidelines, the sudden whistles, even children crying on nearby bleachers make her feel as if something terrible is about to happen in plain sight and she will fail again to stop it.

She carries guilt with a stubborn, private intensity. She knows she called for help. She knows others froze too. Still, she replays the first few seconds over and over, imagining alternate versions of herself-braver, faster, louder. In sessions she speaks carefully, often minimizing before emotion overtakes her. What reaches her most is not only fear but a shaken sense of who she is. She chose forestry because she sees herself as capable, practical, someone who can stay calm outdoors when others cannot. Since that afternoon, she feels split between the competent young woman who hikes miles alone with a map and radio, and the one whose hands stop working when violence erupts in front of her.

In the present, she structures her days around avoiding the sensations she cannot trust. She sleeps lightly, checks locks repeatedly, and keeps her phone volume high at night in case someone needs help. Some mornings she drives to the forest before sunrise and sits in her truck gripping a coffee gone cold, staring at the tree line and trying to gather herself before stepping out. She still loves the woods. But now even among the pines, with wind moving through branches above her, part of her is listening for screams.
